question: Some 300 asylum seekers are reportedly being lodged on appalling conditions at the extraordinary reception centre in the former Zanusso barracks in Oderzo (Treviso). According to trade unions, they are being housed in unheated, overcrowded tensile structures. The boiler is apparently only turned on during inspections by the authorities, leaving migrants in the cold and deprived of hot water the rest of the time1.

This state of affairs, exacerbated by their parlous administrative situation, makes them particularly vulnerable to both having to work in the informal sector and exploitation. This would appear to be a clear breach of Reception Conditions Directive2 and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to ask the Italian authorities for clarification as to compliance with the minimum reception standards laid down in EU law?
How does it intend to ensure that national monitoring mechanisms are effective and cannot be circumvented by ‘smokescreen’ measures?
Does it consider these structural shortcomings and the vulnerability of asylum seekers to be compatible with EU strategies for the prevention of labour exploitation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.3.2026) The Italian Ministry of Interior informed the Commission services that the Prefecture of Treviso has regularly monitored the situation at the reception centre and met with the trade unions. During the last visit, 272 applicants for international protection were being hosted in the centre, which has a capacity for 260.

The Commission was also informed that, while the prefecture is considering replacing the tent structure with housing modules, the criticalities concerning the material reception conditions would have been addressed.

Directive (EU) 2013/331 requires Member States to ensure that accommodation centres guarantee an adequate standard of living and to have in place relevant mechanisms to ensure monitoring and control of reception conditions.

In accordance with Directive (EU) 2024/13462, Member States will have to take into account guidance tools on reception conditions by the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) and will be subject to the EUAA’s new monitoring mechanism established by Regulation (EU) 2021/23033.

As announced in the Asylum and Migration Management Strategy4, there is a need to step up the fight against illegal employment and abuse of third-country workers. The Commission will present in 2026 the state of implementation of the Employers Sanctions Directive and, if needed, propose amendments.

As highlighted in the Quality Jobs Roadmap5, controls and inspections need to be intensified to detect and sanction exploitative employers and protect the rights of third-country workers. As part of the revision of the mandate of the European Labour Authority, the Commission will review how it could better address the challenges related to abuses of working conditions of third-country nationals.
